short_definition: SMART goals are goals written to be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound, which turns vague wishes into clear targets you can plan for and track.
explanation: The SMART framework tests a goal against five criteria. Specific: exactly what you want. Measurable: how you'll know you're progressing. Achievable: realistic given your resources. Relevant: connected to what matters to you. Time-bound: a deadline. 'Get better with money' becomes 'Save 2,000 for an emergency fund by 31 December.'

It matters because vague goals are hard to act on and easy to abandon. A measurable target with a deadline tells you what to do this week and shows whether you're on track, so you can adjust early instead of finding out too late.

The trade-off is that SMART goals can become rigid or too narrow. Targets that are too 'achievable' can limit ambition. Measurable targets can also pull attention toward what's easy to count instead of what's important. Review your goals regularly and update them as your life changes.
example: Example (illustrative numbers only): Vague goal: 'Pay off debt.' SMART version: 'Pay off my 1,200 credit card balance within 6 months by paying 200 a month, tracked in my budget app every payday.' (Interest may add to the total, so check your statement.)
common_mistake: Writing a SMART goal once and never reviewing it, so it stays out of step with real progress or changed circumstances.
title: SMART Goals
